title: Logical outgrowth and changes between proposed and final rules
shortTitle: Logical outgrowth and changes between proposed and final rules
summary: A final rule may respond to comments, but interested people must have received adequate notice of the subjects and alternatives that lead to the final approach.
notes:
The logical-outgrowth requirement asks whether the proposal adequately framed the issues so that affected parties reasonably could anticipate the agency’s eventual course. Long Island Care at Home v. Coke endorses the requirement as part of adequate notice under § 553. The test permits revision through learning from comments, while requiring renewed notice when the final approach moves beyond the reasonably described range.

The assigned Mock v. Garland dispute illustrates the tension. ATF proposed a points worksheet for classifying firearms fitted with stabilizing braces, then adopted a six-factor method after criticism. The majority regarded that change and the new use-related criteria as inadequately forecast. Higginson thought the criticism itself showed that removal of the worksheet and consideration of those issues were foreseeable. The comparison turns on what the notice and actual comments communicated, rather than a rule that any major revision is forbidden or every response to criticism is adequately noticed.
